summary: This unit teaches you to plan, assemble, fix, wire, weatherproof and test LED signs: channel letters, lightboxes, LED strip outlines and programmable message displays. You will learn to size the driver, prevent voltage drop, fix signs securely against Jamaican weather, work safely at height above the public, and protect the electrics from rain, sun and salt. You will also learn to commission a sign, find faults and hand it over to the customer.

blocks.p: LED signs are on shop fronts, pharmacies, gas stations, churches, bars and hotels all over Jamaica. They use far less power than the neon and fluorescent signs they replaced, but they still need careful installation: the right driver, cables that keep the voltage up, fixings that survive a hurricane, and electrics that keep out the rain. This unit is for Level 2 trainees, who do this work as part of a team under a qualified supervisor.

blocks.h: What you must be able to do

head: Task
What it looks like on the job
rows: Plan the installation
Agree the position, fixings, power point and controls with the customer from the drawing; check the wall, approvals, access and weather.
Know the types of sign and their parts
Tell channel letters, lightboxes, strip outlines and message displays apart, and name their modules, strips, drivers and faces.
Choose and size the driver
Match the driver type and voltage to the LEDs, add up the load, allow a margin, and work out the output current.
Prevent voltage drop
Keep runs short, size the feed cables, feed long runs at more than one point, and use 24 V where it helps.
Fix the sign securely
Choose fixings for the wall, check for hidden services, drill and fix as the anchor maker states, and get the sign level.
Work safely at height
Choose and check the access equipment, keep the public clear below, and stop work in bad weather.
Weatherproof and protect the electrics
Use the right IP ratings, glands, drip loops and sealants; earth metal parts; isolate and lock off before any mains work.
Assemble, wire and set the controls
Lay out and fix modules and strip evenly, cut and join strip correctly, observe polarity, and set photocells, time switches and displays.
Test, commission and hand over
Check polarity and shorts dead, measure voltages after switch-on, find faults, and explain the sign and its upkeep to the customer.

ul: JPS supplies **110 V and 220 V at 50 Hz**. The sign's driver changes this to the low-voltage DC the LEDs need.
Signs must survive **hurricane-season** winds (June to November), heavy rain, strong sun that breaks down ordinary plastics, and **salt air** near the coast.
The mains wiring to a sign is installed and tested under the supervision of a qualified, licensed electrician, to the code used in Jamaica. The DC side of the sign is extra-low voltage.

blocks.note: Before anyone works on the mains side of a sign or its driver: switch off, lock off with your own padlock, fix a tag, and prove dead with a tester proved before and after. At the Centre, the DC practicals use a bench supply that only the assessor connects and switches.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: Read the sections in the order a job is done: from the types of sign and planning, through the electrics and fixing, to testing and handover. Then try the practice test and read each explanation.

sections.title: Types of LED sign and their parts

head: Type
What it is
Where it suits
rows: Channel letters
Separate hollow letters, with sides (returns) of aluminium or plastic and a translucent acrylic face, each lit from inside by LED modules. Some are lit from behind to give a 'halo' on the wall.
Shop and company names on a building front; they look smart and can be read from far away
Lightbox (sign box)
A box with a translucent face carrying the printed design, lit evenly from behind by LED modules or strip inside
Smaller shops, menus, roadside signs; cheaper than channel letters
LED strip or neon-flex outline
Flexible LED strip, or strip inside a silicone 'neon' tube, fixed round the edge of a sign, window or building
Bars, restaurants and anywhere that wants to catch the eye at night
Programmable message display
Panels of many LEDs worked by a controller, so that the words, prices and pictures can be changed
Gas stations, pharmacies, churches and schools that change their messages often

head: Part
Description
rows: LED module

A small sealed unit with a few LEDs (often three) and a lens, joined to others on a wire chain. Commonly 12 V DC and about 0.7–1.5 W each, rated about IP65–IP68. Used in channel letters and lightboxes.
LED strip

A flexible printed strip carrying LEDs and resistors, with a sticky back, sold on reels (often 5 m). 12 V or 24 V DC, rated in watts per metre. It may be cut only at the marked cut lines, across the copper pads.
Neon flex
LED strip inside a silicone or PVC diffuser that looks like a neon tube. It has a smallest bend radius that must not be exceeded.
LED driver

The power supply that changes mains AC into the low-voltage DC the LEDs need. Rated in watts, with an output voltage or current, an IP rating, and a class (Class I with an earth terminal, or Class II double insulated).
Face
Usually **opal (milky white) acrylic**, which spreads the light evenly, with printed or translucent vinyl graphics.
Display panels and controller
Message displays are built from LED panels (described by pixel pitch, for example P10 = 10 mm between pixels), powered by 5 V DC supplies that give large currents, and worked by a controller card.
Controls
An isolator, and a photocell, time switch or both; sometimes a contactor or dimmer.

blocks.p: White LEDs come in different **colour temperatures**: warm white (about 3000 K) looks yellowish, cool white (about 6000–6500 K) looks bluish. When you replace modules or strip, match the colour temperature, or the repair will show.

blocks.note: Low-voltage DC does not give a dangerous shock, but it can carry a large current. A short circuit or a poor joint on the DC side can overheat and start a fire, so the DC wiring needs the same care as mains wiring.
blocks.label: Remember

flow: Visit the site with the drawing
Agree with the customer the sign's position, size, lighting and controls, and where the power will come from
Check the wall: what it is made of, whether it is sound, and what fixings it needs
Plan the cable route, the isolator position near the sign, and a dry, shaded, ventilated place for the driver
Check approvals: the landlord, and the local municipal corporation where a permit is needed
Choose the access equipment and plan how to keep the public clear below
Look for hazards: overhead JPS lines, traffic, other signs, fragile roofs
List the materials and tools, write the risk assessment, and agree who does each job
Check the weather forecast and plan the work for calm, dry days

head: Check
Why
rows: Wall type and condition
Hollow block, filled block, concrete, timber or steel each need different fixings; cracked render or loose blocks must be reported
Height and access
Decides between steps, a tower scaffold or a lift, and whether the sidewalk must be closed
Power source
A suitable circuit for the sign, with room for a lockable isolator near it
Driver position
Out of the rain and direct sun, with air round it, and where it can be reached for maintenance
Cable route
Short, protected, entering boxes from below
Hidden services
Cables, pipes and gas lines in the wall where fixings will go
Neighbours and road users
The sign must not dazzle drivers or shine into bedrooms

blocks.note: A sign on a building usually needs the approval of the parish's **municipal corporation**, and a rented building needs the **landlord's** agreement as well as the customer's. Your supervisor or the sign company checks this before work starts. Plan around the hurricane season (June to November): never put up a sign when a storm is forecast.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: Agree **brightness and hours** at the planning stage. A roadside sign that is too bright at night can dazzle drivers and annoy neighbours. Many displays and drivers can be dimmed at night, and the controls can switch the sign off at a set hour.
The **driver** changes the mains AC (110 V or 220 V) into the low-voltage DC that the LEDs need, and protects them. Many drivers accept any supply from about 100 V to 240 V AC; the label says.

head: Driver type
What it gives
Use it for
rows: Constant voltage (CV)
A fixed voltage, usually 12 V or 24 V DC; the current depends on the load
LED strip and modules marked '12 V DC' or '24 V DC', which have their own resistors. The loads are connected in parallel on the output.
Constant current (CC)
A fixed current, such as 350 mA or 700 mA; the voltage changes to suit
High-power LEDs wired in series that are marked with a current, not a voltage

blocks.note: Match the driver to what is printed on the LEDs. A constant-current driver on a 12 V strip, a driver of the wrong voltage, or an old 12 V AC transformer meant for halogen lamps will make LEDs flicker, fail or not light at all.
blocks.label: Remember

flow: Add up the load: modules × watts each, or metres × watts per metre
Match the output voltage (and type) to the LEDs
Allow a margin: load the driver to no more than about 80% of its rating (rating at least load ÷ 0.8)
Choose the next standard size up
Check the IP rating for where it will go
Work out the output current, I = P ÷ V, to size the output cable
Split a large sign into zones, each with its own driver

blocks.p: **Example 1.** A lightbox has 60 modules at 0.72 W, 12 V. Load = 60 × 0.72 = 43.2 W. 43.2 ÷ 0.8 = 54 W, so choose a 60 W, 12 V constant-voltage driver. Output current = 43.2 ÷ 12 = 3.6 A.

**Example 2.** An outline uses 12 m of 24 V strip at 12 W per metre. Load = 12 × 12 = 144 W. 144 ÷ 0.8 = 180 W, so choose a 200 W, 24 V driver, or two smaller drivers feeding half each. Output current = 144 ÷ 24 = 6 A.

ul: A driver run flat out at its full rating gets hot and dies early. A driver far too big costs more and can work poorly at a very light load.
Do not join the outputs of two drivers together unless the maker allows it. Give each driver its own zone.

On the mains side, a driver draws roughly its output power divided by its efficiency (often about 85–90%). For example, 144 W ÷ 0.88 ≈ 164 W, about 1.5 A on 110 V. The label gives the input current. Drivers also draw a surge at switch-on, so the maker limits how many may share one breaker.

blocks.p: DC has a **positive (+)** and a **negative (−)**. The + wire is usually red or marked; the − wire black or striped. Connected the wrong way round, LEDs do not light, and modules without protection can be damaged. Check the polarity at every module, strip and terminal block before switch-on.

For the same power, a low voltage means a high current: **I = P ÷ V**. Every conductor has some resistance, and the voltage lost along it is **V = I × R**. At 12 V a loss of 1 V is over 8% of the supply, enough to make LEDs visibly dimmer.

ul: The LEDs near the feed are bright, and those at the far end are dimmer.
White LEDs at the far end look slightly yellow or pink.
The voltage measured at the last module is well below the voltage at the first.
**In the strip itself.** The copper tracks are thin. A 12 V strip is commonly fed at least every 5 m or so, a 24 V strip about every 10 m; the maker gives the figure for each strip.
**In the feed cable from the driver.** The current flows out along one wire and back along the other, so a 10 m feed has 20 m of conductor in its path.

blocks.h: Example: a 5 A load fed through 10 m of two-core cable at 12 V

head: Copper size
Resistance of 20 m (out and back)
Voltage lost
Share of 12 V
rows: 16 AWG
About 0.26 Ω
About 1.3 V
About 11%
14 AWG
About 0.17 Ω
About 0.83 V
About 7%
12 AWG
About 0.10 Ω
About 0.52 V
About 4%
10 AWG
About 0.066 Ω
About 0.33 V
About 3%

blocks.p: Many makers ask for the drop to be kept within about 5%, and some ask for less. Here 12 AWG or larger would be needed.

blocks.h: How to keep the voltage up

ul: Put the driver **close to the sign**, so the low-voltage feed is short.
Use **thick enough** feed cable for the current and the length.
Keep each run within the length the strip maker allows.
**Feed long runs at more than one point**: at both ends, or every few metres, each with its own cable from the driver.

Use **24 V** instead of 12 V where you can. For the same power it carries half the current, so the volts lost in the same cable are halved, and as a share of the higher voltage the loss is only a quarter.
Use cable rated for outdoor use and resistant to UV (sunlight).
Use two-core cable for the DC feeds, with the + and − cores clearly identified.
Support and clip cables so that no joint takes any strain, and protect them where they could be damaged.
The mains cable to the driver and isolator is chosen and installed to the code by the electrician.

sections.title: Fixing the sign and working at height

head: Wall
Suitable fixings
Take care
rows: Hollow concrete block (common in Jamaica)
Resin (chemical) anchors with mesh sleeves, or anchors made for hollow block; fix into filled cores or solid parts where possible
Many anchor makers say to drill hollow block with the hammer action off, so the thin walls are not broken out: follow the anchor maker
Solid or reinforced concrete, filled block
Expansion (wedge or sleeve) anchors or resin anchors
Keep the maker's edge and spacing distances. If the bit hits reinforcing steel, stop and move the hole.
Timber
Coach screws into solid timber
Find the studs or framing
Steel
Bolts or clamps
Do not weaken the steelwork without approval

blocks.h: Fixing a sign box or bracket

flow: Mark the fixing positions from the template with a tape measure and spirit level
Scan the positions for hidden cables and pipes with a detector
Put on safety glasses, a dust mask and hearing protection
Drill with a hammer drill and a masonry bit of the size and depth the anchor maker states
Clean the dust out of each hole with a pump or brush
Fit the anchors (resin needs its full curing time before loading)
Fit the bracket or sign and tighten to the stated torque
Check that it is level and does not move

ul: Use **enough** fixings of the right size for the sign's weight **and the wind load**. A sign is pushed and pulled hard by gusts.
Near the sea, use **stainless steel or hot-dip galvanised** fixings: salt air rusts plain steel quickly.
Never cut reinforcing steel in concrete without an engineer's approval: it gives the wall its strength.

blocks.note: A badly fixed sign can be torn off in a hurricane and thrown onto people, cars and roofs. Fix every sign as if a storm is coming, check the fixings after every storm, and never take a short cut on the number or size of fixings.
blocks.label: Jamaica

head: Equipment
When to use it
Key checks
rows: Ladder
Short, light work only, such as a quick check
About 75° (1 out for every 4 up); about 1 m above any landing point; tied or footed; three points of contact; never for carrying a sign
Stepladder or podium step
Low work, about 2 m or less
Fully open and locked; on level ground; do not stand on the top step or over-reach
Mobile tower scaffold
Longer jobs at height, such as fixing a lightbox
Put up by a competent person; on firm, level ground; wheels locked; outriggers fitted; full guardrails and toe boards; never moved with anyone on it
Mobile elevating work platform (lift)
High or awkward positions
Trained operator only; harness where the maker requires; ground checked

ul: Close off the sidewalk below with cones, barriers or tape, and keep a person on the ground to keep people out.
Carry tools in a belt, tie them on with lanyards where you can, and lift parts in a bag or on a line. A dropped tool can kill.
Ground crew wear hard hats.
Stop in strong wind, rain or lightning. A large flat sign acts like a sail in a gust.
Look up for **JPS lines** before raising a ladder, tower or sign, and keep well clear.
Wear a hard hat, safety glasses, safety boots and gloves; add a dust mask and hearing protection when drilling.

blocks.p: The **IP** (ingress protection) code shows how well equipment keeps out solids and water. The **first digit** is for dust and solid objects; the **second digit** is for water.

head: Digit
First digit (solids)
Second digit (water)
rows: No protection
No protection
Objects over 1 mm
Splashing water from any direction
Dust-protected
Water jets
Dust-tight
Powerful water jets
Short immersion (usually up to 1 m for 30 minutes)
Continuous immersion, as the maker states

ul: **IP20**: indoor use only, no protection against water.
**IP65**: dust-tight and protected against water jets: a usual minimum for drivers and parts outdoors in the rain.
**IP67**: dust-tight and safe in short immersion: common for outdoor strip and modules.
**IP68**: for long immersion, such as fountains and pools.
Bring cables into boxes **from below or the side**, never through the top, through a **cable gland** of the right size, tightened so that it grips and seals the cable.
Leave a **drip loop** (a low curve) in each cable just before it enters, so that water runs to the bottom of the loop and drips off instead of following the cable in.
Fill unused holes with proper blanking plugs; check that every gasket is seated and every lid is closed tightly.
Where the maker allows, drill small drain holes at the lowest point of a sign box so that any water can escape.
Make joints in rated junction boxes or with the maker's sealed connectors; seal soldered strip joints with adhesive-lined heat-shrink or the maker's end caps. **Never rely on tape.**
Seal round entries and fixings with **neutral-cure** outdoor silicone. The 'vinegar-smelling' (acid-cure) kind gives off acid as it sets, which corrodes copper and electronics.
Use **UV-resistant** cable ties and cable outdoors: strong sun makes ordinary plastic brittle in a few months.

blocks.p: Drivers and LEDs last much longer when they run cool. Do not seal a driver in a small box in the sun: put it in shade where possible, with space for air round it, or in a ventilated, rated enclosure. Fix outdoor strip in aluminium channel, which carries heat away. A driver that is too hot to touch is likely to fail early.

blocks.h: Isolation, earthing and protection on the mains side

ul: The sign is fed from a suitable circuit in the panel, through an **isolator** (disconnect) near the sign that can be locked off. The code used in Jamaica requires a means of disconnecting each sign, normally within sight of it, so that work can be done safely.

**Earth** every metal sign frame and box, and every **Class I** driver (metal case with an earth terminal), with the earth conductor (green, or green and yellow). If a live part touches the metal in a fault, the fault current flows to earth and the protective device trips.
A **Class II** (double-insulated) driver has no earth terminal; any metal frame that mains wiring passes into is still earthed.
Outdoor sign circuits are commonly given **GFCI (RCD) protection**, which trips if current leaks to earth, for example through water. The GFCI adds protection; it never replaces the earth.
The DC negative is never used as an earth, and never joined to the frame unless the maker's instructions say so.

blocks.note: At Level 2 you help with the mains side only under the direct supervision of a qualified electrician, and only after it has been isolated, locked off, tagged and proved dead.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.h: Laying out modules in a lightbox or letter

ul: Follow the drawing: rows of modules spaced **evenly**, starting close to the edges, and in channel letters following the shape of each stroke.

The spacing depends on the depth from the modules to the face. A common rule of thumb is to keep the spacing no more than about the depth of the box; the module maker's chart gives the figures. Too wide a spacing shows as **bright spots and dark bands** on the face.
Clean the backboard with isopropyl alcohol before fixing, and fix each module with its adhesive **and** a screw where the maker allows: adhesive alone can let go in the heat.
Modules on a chain are in **parallel**: each gets the 12 V. The maker gives the largest number of modules on one chain.
Feed each chain or group separately from the driver's output, through a terminal block.
Keep the **polarity** right at every joint, and use the maker's connectors.
Clip the cables neatly so that no joint takes any strain.

Cut **only at the marked cut lines**, across the middle of the copper pads. On 12 V strip these often come every three LEDs (about 50 mm on a 60 LED/m strip); on 24 V strip every six. Cut anywhere else and the LEDs in that group will not light.
Join at the pads by **soldering** (clean, fluxed, quick) or with the maker's **clip-on connectors**. Never twist bare ends together or use tape.
Seal the ends and joints of outdoor strip with the maker's end caps, silicone or adhesive-lined heat-shrink.
Stick strip only to a clean, dry, dust-free surface. Outdoors, fix it in aluminium channel with a diffuser.
Do not bend strip or neon flex more sharply than the maker allows, and never fold it across an LED.

head: Control
What it does
Points to watch
rows: Photocell
Switches the sign on at dusk and off at dawn
Fit it where it sees the sky but not the sign's own light or a street lamp
Time switch
Switches on and off at set times
A simple one loses time in a power cut; one with a battery (power reserve) keeps time
Photocell with a time switch
On at dusk, off at a set hour (for example 11 p.m.)
The usual choice for shop signs
Astronomical time switch
Works out sunset and sunrise for each day of the year
Set the location and the date correctly
Contactor
Lets a small control switch a large sign load
Rated for the drivers' switch-on surge
Dimmer or brightness controller
Lowers the brightness, for example at night
The driver must be a dimmable type that suits the dimmer

ul: New text, prices and pictures are loaded with the **maker's software**, from a computer or phone, by USB stick, cable, Wi-Fi or network.
Set a schedule and the brightness. Many displays dim themselves at night with a built-in light sensor.
The panels run on 5 V DC from power supplies that give large currents, so their cables are thick and their connections must be tight.
Keep the passwords safe and give them to the customer at handover.

sections.title: Testing, commissioning, fault finding and handover

flow: Check every connection against the wiring diagram, and that each is tight
With the supply off, measure across the DC output wiring: there must be no short circuit between + and −
Check the polarity at each module, strip and terminal block
Check the earth continuity of the metal frame
The mains side is tested by a qualified person: insulation resistance, earth continuity, polarity and the GFCI
Only then does the authorised person switch on (at the Centre, the assessor connects the bench supply)

ul: Every module or strip section lights, evenly and in the same colour.
Measure the voltage at the first and last module of each run, work out the drop, and record it.
After the sign has run for a while, check that the driver is warm but not too hot to touch.
Test the controls: cover the photocell to make it 'dark'; set the time switch and check that it switches.
Label the isolator and the driver, and record all the readings.

flow: Ask the customer what happened and when (after rain, a storm, a power cut, a knock?)
Look at the sign from the ground
Isolate, lock off, tag and prove dead before opening anything
Inspect: water, burnt or loose connections, crushed parts
Test: continuity, polarity and, with the supply restored by an authorised person, voltages
Repair with matching parts and reseal
Restore the supply, test, and record what was found and done

head: Symptom
Likely causes
rows: The whole sign is dark
Isolator or breaker off, GFCI tripped, photocell or time switch, failed driver, or a mains wiring fault
The sign blinks on and off, and the driver ticks
A short circuit or overload: the driver cuts out and tries again every second or so. Look for a crushed module, a pinched wire or water in a connector.
One section is dark
A connector or wire at the start of that section, a failed module at the start of the chain, or strip cut in the wrong place
A single module is dark
That module has failed: replace it with a matching one
The far end is dim or yellowish
Voltage drop: add a feed, use thicker cable or a shorter run, or go to 24 V
Flickering
A loose connection, an overloaded or failing driver, the wrong type of driver, or a dimmer that does not suit the driver
The GFCI trips after rain
Water in the driver box or a connector, or a damaged cable
A section is a different white
Replacement modules of a different colour temperature
The sign is on in daytime or switches at the wrong time
A faulty or shaded photocell, or a time switch that lost time in a power cut

ul: Walk the customer round the finished sign.
Give them the driver data sheets, the wiring diagram, the test record and any warranty.
Show them how to use the controls, including resetting the time switch after a power cut, and where the isolator is.
Tell them who to call, and what not to do (for example, never hose water into the sign or open the driver box).

blocks.p: A sensible routine, about every six months and after every storm: look for dark or dim LEDs, water inside, loose or rusted fixings, cracked or faded faces, damaged cables and glands, and clean the face. Check that the driver has air round it and that the controls are switching at the right times.

Old modules, strip and drivers are **e-waste**: put them in the Centre's e-waste collection or hand them to an approved collector. Never burn them or put them in a gully. Collect off-cuts, cable ties and packaging, and leave the site clean.
Tick each statement only when you can do it without looking at the notes.

ul: I can describe channel letters, lightboxes, strip outlines and message displays and say where each suits.
I can name the parts of an LED sign, including modules, strip, neon flex, drivers and faces.
I can plan a sign installation, including the wall, power, isolator, driver position, approvals, access and weather.
I can tell constant-voltage and constant-current drivers apart and choose the right one.
I can add up a sign's load, allow a margin, choose a driver size and work out its output current.
I can explain voltage drop, recognise it and use at least four ways to prevent it.
I can choose fixings for hollow block, concrete, timber and steel and fix a sign level and secure.
I can choose and check access equipment and keep the public safe below.
I can explain the IP code and choose suitable ratings for outdoor work.
I can make cable entries weatherproof with glands, drip loops and the right sealant.
I can explain why metal frames and Class I drivers are earthed and why GFCI protection is used.
I can lay out modules evenly, cut and join LED strip correctly, and keep the polarity right.
I can set up photocells, time switches and message displays.
I can carry out the dead checks and commissioning checks, and record the readings.
I can find common faults, hand over a sign and describe its maintenance.

head: Figure
What it is
rows: 12 V and 24 V DC
Usual voltages for LED modules and strip; 5 V for message display panels
Load ÷ 0.8
Smallest driver rating to choose (load no more than about 80%)
I = P ÷ V
Output current: 54 W at 12 V is 4.5 A
About 5%
A common limit for voltage drop; some makers ask for less
About every 5 m (12 V), 10 m (24 V)
Typical feed intervals for LED strip; follow the maker
IP65 / IP67
Usual minimums outdoors: water jets / short immersion
1 in 4 (about 75°); 1 m above
Ladder angle, and height above a landing point
June to November
Hurricane season
About 3000 K / 6500 K
Warm white / cool white

terms: Channel letters
Separate hollow letters, each lit from inside by LEDs.
Colour temperature
How warm (yellowish) or cool (bluish) a white light looks, in kelvin (K).
Constant-current driver
A driver that gives a fixed current, for LEDs in series that are rated by current.
Constant-voltage driver
A driver that keeps its output voltage steady, as most 12 V and 24 V strips and modules need.
Cable gland
A fitting that grips and seals a cable where it enters a box.
Drip loop
A low curve left in a cable so that water drips off before reaching the entry.
Driver
The unit that changes mains AC into the low-voltage DC that LEDs need.
Expansion anchor
A bolt that grips by spreading out inside a hole drilled in concrete.
IP rating
Ingress protection code: how well equipment keeps out solids (first digit) and water (second digit).
Isolator
A switch that cuts off the supply to the sign and can be locked off for safe work.
LED module
A small sealed unit of a few LEDs and a lens, joined to others on a wire chain.
LED strip
A flexible, sticky-backed strip of LEDs sold on reels and cut to length at marked lines.
Lightbox
A sign box whose whole face is lit from behind by LEDs inside it.
Neon flex
LED strip inside a diffuser that looks like a neon tube.
Opal acrylic
Milky-white plastic sheet that spreads light evenly across a sign face.
Photocell
A light sensor that switches a sign on at dusk and off at dawn.
Polarity
Which wire is positive and which is negative on the DC side.
Time switch
A control that switches a sign on and off at set times.
Voltage drop
The voltage lost along a conductor because of its resistance.

c1.title: Channel letters for a Savanna-la-Mar pharmacy
c1.text: A pharmacy in Savanna-la-Mar, Westmoreland, has ordered channel letters for its shop front. The letters hold 36 LED modules, each rated 12 V DC, 1.5 W. The front wall is hollow concrete block, and the letters will be about 3.5 m above the sidewalk. Trainee Damion is on the installation team with Mr Courtney Bailey. The drivers in the van are all 12 V constant-voltage types: 50 W, 60 W, 75 W and 400 W.

c2.title: An LED outline for a Discovery Bay restaurant
c2.text: A restaurant in Discovery Bay, St Ann, wants a white LED strip outline round its roof edge, a run of 16 m in all, lit from dusk until 1 a.m. The installer has IP67 12 V strip with cut marks every 50 mm. On a trial with the strip fed at one end only, the far end looks dim and slightly yellow.

c3.title: A lightbox over a Half Way Tree sidewalk
c3.text: A shoe store in Half Way Tree, St Andrew, is having a 1.8 m × 0.9 m lightbox fixed 4.5 m up its reinforced concrete front wall, above a busy sidewalk. Trainee Tashauna and her supervisor, Mr Marlon Gordon, will work from a mobile scaffold tower. It is September, and gusty winds are forecast for the afternoon.

c4.title: Rain trouble at an Annotto Bay sign
c4.text: A hardware store in Annotto Bay, St Mary, had a lightbox installed last year. Since the rains began, the GFCI on the sign circuit trips most evenings. Trainee Romaine finds that the driver, marked IP20 and Class I, was fitted inside a small sealed plastic box on top of the lightbox, in full sun, with its cable coming in through the lid. The lightbox frame is aluminium.

c5.title: A blinking canopy sign in Spaldings
c5.text: A gas station in Spaldings, Clarendon, has a lit canopy sign and a programmable LED price display. One evening the canopy sign starts blinking on and off about once a second, and the attendant hears a ticking from its driver. The next day trainee Kevin finds a crushed LED module where a delivery truck scraped the canopy. Since last week's power cut, the canopy sign's time switch has also been running two hours late.

questions.q: What is the total load of the modules?
questions.why: Total load = number of modules × watts each = 36 × 1.5 = 54 W. 4.5 is the current in amps at 12 V (54 ÷ 12), not the load, and 648 multiplies by the voltage as well.

questions.q: Which driver from the van is the best choice?
o: The 75 W driver
The 50 W driver
The 60 W driver
The 400 W driver
questions.why: A driver should run at no more than about 80% of its rating: 54 ÷ 0.8 = 67.5 W, so 75 W is the right size (about 72% loaded). The 50 W driver is too small, the 60 W one would run at 90% and get hot, and the 400 W one is costly, bulky and can work poorly at so light a load.

questions.q: At full load, how much current does the 12 V feed from the driver to the letters carry?
questions.why: I = P ÷ V = 54 ÷ 12 = 4.5 A. This is why low-voltage feeds need thicker cables than their power alone suggests. 0.49 A would be the current if 54 W were drawn at 110 V.

questions.q: What should Damion do before he drills the fixing holes?
o: Drill a test hole in the middle of the wall
Take down the sidewalk barrier to have more room
Wet the wall so that the dust does not rise
Scan the wall for hidden cables and pipes
questions.why: A drill bit through a hidden cable can give a shock or cut the supply, and one through a pipe floods the wall. Scan the marked positions with a cable and pipe detector, check the building's drawings, and move a fixing if needed.

questions.q: How should the 16 m run be fed?
o: At one end only, but from a driver twice the size
In the middle only, leaving both ends unfed
From the driver at both ends and in the middle
At the far end only, so that the dim part gets power
questions.why: The strip's thin tracks lose voltage along a long run, so 12 V strip is usually fed about every 5 m. Feeding both ends and the middle, each with its own cable from the driver, keeps every part near 12 V. A bigger driver does not help: the loss is in the strip, not the driver.

questions.q: To fit a corner, a length of strip is cut halfway between two cut marks. What happens?
o: That cut group of LEDs will not light
The whole strip will now run at 24 V
The LEDs beside the cut will glow brighter
Nothing, as the strip can be cut anywhere
questions.why: On 12 V strip the LEDs are wired in small groups, often three LEDs and a resistor, between cut marks. Cutting through a group breaks it, so those LEDs stay dark. Cut only on the marked lines, across the copper pads, and join there.

questions.q: What does the '7' in IP67 tell the installer?
o: It can be kept under water all the time
It is protected only against splashing water
It can survive short immersion in water
It is dust-tight but not protected from water
questions.why: The second digit of the IP code is for water: 4 is splashing, 5 water jets, 6 powerful jets, 7 short immersion (usually up to 1 m for 30 minutes), and 8 continuous immersion as the maker states. The first digit, 6, means dust-tight.

questions.q: Which control best switches the outline on at dusk and off at 1 a.m.?
o: A photocell on its own, facing up at the sky
A photocell together with a time switch
A push button beside the kitchen door
A dimmer fitted on the driver's output
questions.why: The photocell switches the outline on when it gets dark, whatever the season, and the time switch switches it off at the set hour. A photocell on its own would leave it on until dawn, and a dimmer only changes the brightness.

questions.q: Before Tashauna climbs the tower, what must be checked?
o: That the wheels are free, so it can be moved with her on it
Only the top platform, since the frame is steel
That it leans slightly towards the wall for support
Wheels locked, outriggers fitted, guardrails in place
questions.why: A mobile tower must stand on firm, level ground with its wheels locked, its outriggers (stabilisers) fitted and full guardrails and toe boards round the platform. It must never lean on the wall, and it is never moved with anyone on it.

questions.q: Strong gusts arrive while the lightbox is half lifted on the tower. What should happen?
o: Tie it to the guardrail and carry on working
Stop, lower and secure the sign, and come down
Lean the tower against the wall to steady it
Hurry to finish fixing it before the rain starts
questions.why: A large flat sign acts like a sail in a gust and can pull people off the tower or fall onto the sidewalk. Stop the lift, get the sign down and secured, come down, and finish when the wind has dropped.

questions.q: At 30 mm deep, Tashauna's masonry bit hits steel inside the concrete. What should she do?
o: Change to a metal-cutting bit and drill through
Stop, and move the hole as she is directed
Fit the anchor in the shallow hole anyway
Hammer the anchor in until it bends to fit
questions.why: The steel is reinforcing bar, which gives the wall its strength; it must not be cut without an engineer's approval. An anchor in a shallow hole cannot hold its rated load. Move the fixing as the supervisor directs, keeping the anchor maker's spacing and edge distances.

questions.q: What is the most likely reason the GFCI trips after rain?
o: Rain cools the driver, so it takes more power
The LEDs draw more current when it is wet
Water gets in and leaks current to earth
The GFCI is too sensitive and should come out
questions.why: A GFCI trips when current leaks to earth. Water running down the cable into the lid entry reaches the driver's mains terminals and gives that leakage path. The cure is to keep the water out, never to remove the GFCI.

questions.q: What is wrong with the driver and where it was put?
o: An IP20 driver is fine outdoors, sealed in a box
The driver just needs painting black to shed its heat
An indoor (IP20) driver, overheating in a sealed box
The driver is too large and should be a smaller size
questions.why: IP20 means no protection against water, so the driver belongs indoors or in a properly rated enclosure. Sealed in a small box in the sun, it also cannot lose its heat and will fail early. Fit a driver rated IP65 or higher, in shade where possible, with the cable entering from below through a gland and a drip loop.

questions.q: The new driver is also Class I. What must be connected?
o: The earth conductor to the DC positive output
The DC negative to the frame instead of earth
Nothing more, since the GFCI protects against shock
The earth conductor to the driver and the frame
questions.why: A Class I driver has a metal case and an earth terminal, and the aluminium frame can become live in a fault. Both must be earthed so that a fault trips the protective device. The GFCI adds protection; it does not replace the earth, and the DC side is never used as the earth.

questions.q: What is the most likely cause of the blinking and the ticking?
o: The supply frequency is too low for this kind of driver
The driver is cutting out and restarting on a short
The LEDs are still warming up, which is normal at first
The photocell is switching the sign on and off each second
questions.why: Many drivers protect themselves from a short circuit by switching off and trying again every second or so, which makes the sign blink and the driver tick. The crushed module has probably shorted its + and − wires. Isolate, replace it, and check the rest of the chain.

questions.q: How should Kevin choose the replacement module?
o: Same voltage, power and colour as the others
A 24 V module, because it has less voltage drop
A brighter module to make up for the older ones
Any 12 V module, since all of them are alike
questions.why: Modules on one chain must match the driver's voltage, and they should match the others' power and colour temperature, or the repaired part will look brighter, dimmer or a different white. A 24 V module will not light properly on a 12 V chain.

questions.q: What would stop the time switch going wrong after every power cut?
o: A larger driver that stores energy during cuts
A GFCI that resets itself when power returns
A time switch with a battery backup
A photocell placed in the sign's own light
questions.why: A simple time switch stops during a power cut and is then late by the length of the cut. One with a battery or power reserve keeps time through outages. An astronomical time switch with a reserve also follows the changing sunset times.

questions.q: On a 12 V run, a trainee measures 11.9 V at the first module and 10.6 V at the last. What does this show?
o: A normal result: all strips lose about a third
The last module is a different colour from the rest
The driver is faulty and must be replaced at once
About 11% drop: add a feed or use thicker cable
questions.why: The drop is 11.9 − 10.6 = 1.3 V, about 11% of 12 V, well above the 5% or so most makers allow. Feed the far end separately, use thicker feed cable or a shorter run, or move to 24 V. The driver is fine: it gives 11.9 V at the start.

questions.q: Which sealant should be used round cable entries and modules on an outdoor sign?
o: Ordinary wood glue, spread thickly round the entry
Insulating tape wound round several times
The vinegar-smelling silicone used in bathrooms
Neutral-cure outdoor silicone, as the maker says
questions.why: Acid-cure silicone gives off acetic acid (the vinegar smell) as it sets, which corrodes copper and electronics. Neutral-cure silicone made for outdoor use does not. Wood glue breaks down in rain, and tape peels off in sun and heat.

questions.q: Why should stainless steel or hot-dip galvanised fixings be used for a sign on a Montego Bay sea front?
o: Salt air makes plain steel rust quickly
They make a better earth for the sign frame
They are lighter than plain steel fixings
They need no holes drilled for them
questions.why: Salt spray rusts plain and zinc-plated steel fast, and a rusted fixing can let a sign fall, especially in a storm. Stainless steel or hot-dip galvanised fixings last far longer by the sea. Earthing is done with an earth conductor, not with the fixings.
